note: Faults are injected by code into real AI drafts; each copies a failure type from the record. The rules are unchanged since the first commit. Agent answers are recorded and replayable.

cases.title: End time changed in every language

agents_named.issue: The alert extends the hazard end time beyond what the bulletin supports. NCM says conditions run until 19:00 this evening, but the alert says 21:00 in both the headline and the description.

Neither the English nor the Arabic phone text tells the public what to do. Both describe the hazard (dust and sand, visibility under 2,000 m), its duration and its source, but give no protective action, so the first page cannot carry one.

cases.title: End time changed in the Arabic only

agents_named.issue: The two required languages contradict each other on when the hazard ends. English says 19:00 and Arabic says 21:00, so Arabic and English readers get different information from the same alert.
Time mismatch: the English end time is 19:00, but the Arabic headline and description both say 21:00. Machine translation has changed a critical number.

cases.title: Arabic protective action reversed ('no precautions, drive normally')
cases.copies: translation error in the action (FCC-23-88, FCC-DA-25-12)

agents_named.issue: The Arabic instruction reverses the protective action. English tells people to take extra care, especially when driving on open roads, because visibility may drop. The Arabic reads 'There is no need to take any precautions, and you can drive normally.' Arabic readers would be told the opposite of the call to action. This is the exact failure the knowledge base warns about for machine-translated calls to action.

cases.title: Severity inflated to Extreme / Observed

agents_named.issue: Severity is overstated. CAP 'Extreme' means an extraordinary threat to life or property, and the headline says 'EXTREME DANGER'. The NCM bulletin describes fresh to strong winds with visibility below 2,000 m in some areas and only urges the public to exercise caution, especially when driving. That fits a possible threat (Moderate), not an extraordinary one.

Severity mismatch between the two headlines. The English opens with "EXTREME DANGER:" and the Arabic headline has no equivalent, so the two audiences receive different severity signals. The drafter cannot simply add or remove the label: the body text describes an advisory-level hazard (take extra care), so the English label itself may be wrong. A person must decide the intended severity.

cases.title: Unverified rumour added (dam burst)

agents_named.issue: The description repeats an unverified social media rumour (dam burst near Al Ain) as fact and tells people to leave the area. No verified input supports it, and it is not part of the NCM dust bulletin.

The message mixes two hazards. A second hazard, a dam burst with an evacuation instruction, is attached at the end of the dust alert and attributed only to 'Reports say'. A person must decide whether it is confirmed and whether it should go out as its own alert, with its hazard and action on page 1. It should not be buried on the last page of a weather alert.

cases.title: Invented hazard added (flash floods)

agents_named.issue: The description says flash flooding is expected in low-lying areas. The verified NCM bulletin covers only dusty northwesterly winds and reduced visibility. The only flood-related input is an unverified social media rumour about a dam near Al Ain. An unsupported, unverified hazard should not appear in the alert.

A second, potentially more dangerous hazard (flash flooding) is stated only in the final sentence. It lands on the last page (page 3 in English, page 7 in Arabic) and is not reflected on the first page.

cases.title: Invented places added (Dubai, Sharjah)

agents_named.issue: The description adds specific places (Dubai and Sharjah) that the verified NCM bulletin does not name. The bulletin only says 'various areas across the UAE' and 'some coastal and inland areas'. This is an unsupported location claim in the alert.
The named affected areas come last, after the source line, so they fall on the final page (page 3 in en, page 7 in ar). Readers of page 1 may not learn that Dubai and Sharjah are affected.

cases.title: Target area widened to the whole country

agents_named.issue: The alert targets the whole country, but the area drawn for event uae-dust-2026-03-04 covers only coastal and inland Abu Dhabi. The alert area overreaches the requested area.

cases.title: Area description says 'All emirates', codes unchanged

agents_named.issue: The alert's areaDesc claims 'All emirates', but the requested area for this event is only 'Coastal and inland areas, Abu Dhabi (demo zone)'. The geocode AUH-COAST-INLAND also covers only that requested zone. The description therefore overstates the area being alerted and contradicts the codes.

cases.title: Arabic version missing

agents_named.issue: Arabic, a required language, is missing. The phone_text has only an English entry, but the profile requires both Arabic (ar) and English (en), and UAE handset specifications require alerts in both.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The alert tells the public to disregard the weather alert and that no action is needed. The verified NCM bulletin says blowing dust and reduced visibility are ongoing until 19:00 and urges caution. The alert therefore contradicts the verified hazard and could lead people to drop precautions during an active warning. Whether an earlier alert was actually erroneous cannot be confirmed from the inputs, so a person must decide.

The certainty, urgency and severity fields describe an observed, immediate hazard. The headline and description say the alert was sent in error. The alert therefore gives contradictory signals about whether the hazard exists.

The headline says this message corrects or withdraws an earlier alert, but msgType is 'Alert' and references is null, so it does not identify which alert it corrects. The system also shows no earlier alerts, so recipients cannot tell what to disregard.

cases.title: Sender not in the issuer register

agents_named.issue: The sender is not an authorised issuer. 'unknown-sender@nadhir.example' does not appear in the issuer register, yet the alert is a live Actual Public alert for a real event. Only authorised entities may send warning messages. The drafter should not simply swap in the registered identity, because that would misstate who the originator is.

cases.title: English protective action made unsafe

agents_named.issue: The instruction contradicts the verified NCM bulletin. NCM urged the public to exercise caution, especially when driving on open roads, because blowing dust reduces visibility. The alert instead says no precautions are needed and to drive as normal, which understates the hazard the bulletin describes.

The protective action is reversed between languages. English: 'No special precautions are needed; drive as normal.' Arabic: 'Take extra care, especially when driving on open roads, as visibility may drop due to blowing dust.' Arabic readers would be told to act differently from English readers. This cannot be fixed by retranslating, because the English instruction itself sits oddly with a hazard that cuts visibility below 2,000 m. The issuing authority must decide the correct action; then both languages should be made to state it identically and be checked by a human Arabic reviewer.
The Arabic instruction adds an updates link (https://alerts.example.ae) that does not appear anywhere in the English text. This is content present in one language only.

cases.title: Arabic text made far too long

agents_named.issue: The Arabic phone text is 20 pages (UCS-2, 799 characters), over the 15-page maximum for a CBS message, so it cannot be sent as one cell broadcast. The cause is the advice sentence ('ننصح الجميع بمتابعة النشرات الجوية...') repeated three times word for word.

cases.title: End time changed in the Arabic only

agents_named.issue: The Arabic instruction contradicts the English protective action. The English says 'Drive with extreme caution. Keep a safe distance and follow reduced speed limits in fog.' The Arabic means 'There is no need to take any precautions, and you can drive normally.' This tells the public to do the opposite of the intended action during a zero-visibility fog event.

cases.title: Severity inflated to Extreme / Observed

agents_named.issue: Severity 'Extreme' and the headline prefix 'EXTREME DANGER' go beyond the bulletin. NCM issued a fog warning urging motorists to drive with caution. It does not describe an extraordinary threat to life or property, and 'EXTREME DANGER' does not appear in the bulletin.

The English headline begins with the severity prefix 'EXTREME DANGER:', but the Arabic headline starts directly with 'تحذير من الضباب'. Arabic readers lose the extreme-danger signal that English readers get.

cases.title: Unverified rumour added (dam burst)

agents_named.issue: The description adds a report of a dam burst near Al Ain and orders people to leave the area. No verified input mentions this; the only hazard source is the NCM fog warning. This adds an unverified report and a different hazard to the alert.

Both language versions end with an unrelated, unattributed report of a dam burst near Al Ain and an evacuation order. Only the National Center for Meteorology is cited as source, and that is for the fog. Handsets will show this evacuation order with emergency status, so people could act on an unverified claim. If the dam report is true, it is buried on the last page of a fog warning.

cases.title: Invented hazard added (flash floods)

agents_named.issue: The description says flash flooding is expected in low-lying areas. The NCM bulletin covers only fog and reduced visibility and says nothing about flooding. This adds an unsupported second hazard to the alert.

cases.title: Invented places added (Dubai, Sharjah)

agents_named.issue: The alert adds affected places that the NCM bulletin does not name. The bulletin limits the fog and low-visibility warning to western regions, but the description also says Dubai and Sharjah are affected. No verified input supports that.

cases.title: Target area widened to the whole country

agents_named.issue: The alert targets the whole UAE (UAE-ALL), but the area requested for event uae-fog-2026-02-17 is the Western region (AUH-WEST). The alert's own headline also limits the hazard to western regions. Sending it nationally would over-alert people outside the affected area.

cases.title: Area description says 'All emirates', codes unchanged

agents_named.issue: The alert's areaDesc ('All emirates') does not match the area requested for this event or the alert's own geocode (DEMO-ZONE/AUH-WEST). The public-facing area description therefore claims a much wider area than the one targeted.

cases.title: Arabic version missing

agents_named.issue: The required language Arabic (ar) is missing. The only phone text is English, so Arabic-reading recipients in the UAE would get no alert they can read.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The description says an earlier alert was sent in error. No event input reports such an error. The verified NCM bulletin confirms a live fog hazard over this period, so the alert contradicts the bulletin and rests on an unverified claim.

The headline tells the public to disregard an earlier alert, but msgType is "Alert" and references is null. A correction must be a Cancel or Update that points to the message it corrects. No earlier alerts from this system exist, so it is unclear which alert is being retracted, and a stand-alone Actual alert like this could confuse the public.

cases.title: Sender not in the issuer register
English protective action made unsafe

agents_named.issue: The instruction contradicts the verified NCM bulletin. The bulletin urges motorists to take extreme caution, keep a safe distance and follow modified speed limits. The alert tells them no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. Since the instruction is the recommended action for recipients, this reverses what the hazard authority advises.

The protective action contradicts itself across languages. The English tells drivers that no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. The Arabic tells them to drive with extreme caution, keep a safe distance and observe reduced speed limits. For a warning that visibility may drop to zero, the English instruction appears to be wrong, and the Arabic does not translate it. The issuing authority must decide which instruction is authoritative before either version is sent.

cases.title: Arabic text made far too long

agents_named.issue: The Arabic text is 20 pages long, above the 15-page cell broadcast maximum, so it cannot be sent as one message. The cause is the advice paragraph (ننصح الجميع بمتابعة النشرات الجوية...) appearing three times in full.

cases.title: Drill sent as a live alert

agents_named.issue: The context is an exercise or drill, but the alert carries status "Actual" and the console environment is live. Sent as is, the drill would reach the public as a real alert, which is the false-alarm pattern seen in Hawaii. Nothing in the headline marks it as an exercise either.

cases.title: 'This is not a drill' inside a drill

agents_named.issue: The description ends with 'This is not a drill.' The event context and the alert status both mark this as an exercise, and no input supports presenting it as a real event. In an Exercise message this sentence could lead the public to treat a drill as a live warning.

The text is marked EXERCISE / تمرين and refers to a demo zone, yet ends with 'This is not a drill.' / 'هذا ليس تمريناً.' A reader on a handset gets contradictory signals about whether the alert is real.

The Arabic, like the English, contradicts itself on whether the alert is real. It opens with 'تمرين' (exercise) and ends with 'هذا ليس تمريناً' (this is not an exercise/drill). The translation is faithful, but Arabic readers cannot tell whether to act. Mixing exercise labels with 'this is not a drill' contributed to the Hawaii false alert. Whether this is an exercise or a live alert is a decision for a person, not the translator.
